work.title: History of Mar Qardagh
work.edition: Machine translation (claude-opus-5-5, Patristica, 2026-10-30) of: Paul Bedjan Acta martyrum et sanctorum 2; TEI by J. E. Walters, Digital Syriac Corpus (syriaccorpus.org 577)

paragraphs.text: The story of the triumphs of Mar Qardagh, the victorious martyr.

My beloved: the stories of the martyrs and saints of our Lord Jesus Christ are a great benefit to the holy Church. They are spiritual nourishment for the holy congregations of the cross, and an adornment to the lofty beauty of Christianity, which is fashioned in the likeness of the Son of God. They are heavenly wealth for all the generations who enter the holy Church through the spiritual birth of baptism. They are a polished mirror in which the discerning see the ineffable beauty of Christ. They are treasures of righteousness for the children of the Church, who are invited to the heavenly kingdom, and through them the fire of Christ's love is kindled in the souls of believers. Whoever longs to read them and to meditate on them constantly is a beloved son of the saints, and through him the glories of those who are in God are proclaimed.

(1) Trusting in divine power,
a sinful servant now begins
to write the story of the [?]
of Mar Qardagh, sweet of name,
who came from the Assyrian land
and from the line of Nimrod.
Strengthen me, Lord, with your strength,
that by it I may reach the end.

So, my beloved, I wish to tell you of the wondrous victories and great contests of the athlete of righteousness, the holy martyr Mar Qardagh, at whose great contests in martyrdom the angels marveled and men were amazed. This holy Mar Qardagh came from a great family, of the stock of the kingdom of the Assyrians. His father traced his descent from the renowned line of the house of Nimrod, and his mother from the renowned line of the house of Sennacherib. He was born of pagan parents who were lost in the error of Magianism. His father was a man well known in the kingdom and renowned among the Magi, and his name was Gushnawi. The holy Mar Qardagh was handsome in appearance, large in build and strong in body, and he had a spirit skilled in battle. He held fast and vigorously to the error of paganism, and was praised throughout the whole region of the Persians for his devotion to it. When he was about twenty-five years old, Shapur, king of the Persians, heard of his excellence and valor, and sent for him with great honor to come to his court. When he obeyed and came into his presence, and the king saw the beauty of his appearance and the strength

of his body, he was greatly delighted with him. He ordered him to perform in the stadium before all the nobles of the kingdom by shooting arrows at a small target fixed on top of a tall pole. They brought a bow and five arrows from the king's armory. When he shot the five arrows at the target, all of them lodged in a single spot, and he was praised by the king and by all his nobles. The next day the king ordered him to come to the stadium and play ball with him together with the rest of his nobles. When this took place, the king and his nobles were greatly amazed at him. On the third day the king went out hunting with a hundred nobles and three hundred horsemen. He ordered Qardagh to ride with him on a horse from the royal stables and to go before him at the head of those who carried the king's weapons. As they were about to enter a forest, they saw ahead of them a doe running with her fawn. At once the king cried out: "Raise your hand to the bow with all your strength, young Qardagh, and show your [?]!" He quickly took an arrow, set it to the bow, drew it with force, and with a single arrow brought down both the doe and her fawn. Then the king cried with a loud voice: "Long live Qardagh! Live and rejoice in your youth, and let us

rejoice in your victories!" As soon as the king returned from the hunt, he gave orders, and they presented Qardagh with great gifts. He made him viceroy of Assyria and appointed him marzban from the river Tormara as far as the city of Nisibis. He sent him off in state, sending with him great gifts and honors for his father as well. When he had settled in the regions under his authority, the Christian people were deeply shaken because of him, for they knew his tireless zeal for the error of Magianism. Fervent prayer was offered to God for him throughout the whole Church, that he who can do all things would quench his fury and not allow him to stir up persecution against the Christians. For they were being severely persecuted in the reign of Shapur, who thirsted for the blood of the saints. When Qardagh came to his house in Arbela, the city of the Assyrians, he held a great feast for the pagan gods, paid great honor to Magianism, and gave lavish gifts to the fire temples. After a few days he began to build a fortress and buildings on a hill called Melqi. Within two years he had built and completed a strong fortress and a fine house, and below the hill he built a fire temple at great expense and installed Magi in it for the service of the fire. While he was building

that fortress, one night as he slept, he saw in a dream a young man, a horseman, clad and girded in his armor, mounted on a horse and standing over him. He prodded him in the side with the butt of his spear and said to him, "Qardagh." He answered, "Here I am." The horseman said to him, "Know for certain that in front of this fortress you are to die as a martyr for Christ." Qardagh said to him, "Who are you, that you foretell these things to me?" The blessed one said, "I am Sergius, the servant of Christ. I am not practicing divination on you, as you suppose. I have only told you beforehand what is to come, just as Christ my Lord made it known to me." When Qardagh woke from his sleep, he was seized with great fear, and he told the dream to his mother in private. His mother said to him, "Be careful, my son, not to trouble the Christian people. I know it to be true that they are people who worship the one true God, and it was their God who showed you this dream." But he paid no attention. Now there was a blessed man named Abdisho, who lived in a cave on a mountain in the region of Beth Bgash. He was a man great in his way of life, and he delighted in divine

revelations. The Lord said to him in a vision: "Arise, go down and show yourself to Qardagh the marzban, for through you I will catch him for my household. He has much to suffer for my name." So the blessed Abdisho arose, took his staff in his hand, carried the holy Gospel in a small bag, and went down as he had been commanded. One day, as Qardagh was going out to the stadium to play ball, the holy Abdisho met him, cut across the road in front of him and passed on. When Qardagh saw him pass in front of him, he grew very angry and said to those who were with him, "This man is a bad omen." He ordered two servants to strike holy Mar Abdisho in the face. When they had beaten him cruelly, he ordered him to be held under guard until he should decide what was to be done with him. Qardagh went back to his house, and after staying there a little while he rose and mounted again to go to the stadium. But the holy Abdisho, burning with zeal for God, raised his hand, made the sign of the cross and said: "Lord, mighty God, show him your glory and reveal your power to him, so that he may know that you are the true God and there is no other besides you, as you showed me in the revelation." When they reached the stadium and began to drive the ball, galloping on their horses, the ball stuck fast to the ground, and

they could not move it from its place. At once Qardagh ordered one of the servants to dismount, pick up the ball in his hand and throw it far away. But when he lifted it from the ground and hurled it with force, it fell down at his feet. All his servants tried this one after another, and accomplished nothing. Then they were astonished and said, "Truly that man who met us is a sorcerer, and he has bound our ball with his sorceries and ruined our sport." One of them spoke up and said, "While we were getting ready to ride, I saw that man raise his right hand and make the sign of the Christians' cross, and his lips were moving as though he were whispering something." Then the marzban turned back and went into his house, astonished and bewildered at what had happened, he and all who were with him. As soon as he sat down, he gave orders, and they brought holy Abdisho before him. He questioned him angrily and said, "Where are you from, man? And who is your master?" The blessed Abdisho answered him, "As I have heard from my fathers, they were from Haza, a village in the land of the Assyrians. And because they were Christians,

they were driven out by the erring pagans, and went and settled in Tamanon, a village in the land of the Kurds. As for me, I have no known place or dwelling of my own, for I have heard from Christ my Lord, who came and saved us by his holy death, that he had nowhere to lay his head, though heaven and earth, and all things above and below, are his, and he holds, governs and preserves them. My master is the one to whom I offer praise without ceasing and render thanks: God our Maker and Provider, who created us in his image and made us in his likeness, who saved us through his Only-begotten, who put on our body, and who gave us knowledge and understanding, so that we should not regard creatures as gods, nor give the worship that is due to him alone to creatures that came into being and were established by him—as you erring pagans do." When Qardagh heard this, he grew very angry and ordered the saint to be struck on the mouth. As the blessed Abdisho bitterly endured it, his eyes were fixed on heaven, and he silently prayed to God to complete in that servant of his what he had told him in the revelation. Qardagh said to him angrily, "Why do you call

us worshipers of creatures, you foolish old man?" The blessed Abdisho was silent and gave him no answer. Qardagh said to him, "Will you not answer me? Do you not know that I have authority over your death and your life?" The blessed Abdisho said to him, "I suppose, my lord, that someone who is struck on the mouth is being taught that he ought not to speak, and for this reason I gave Your Greatness no answer. But what you said, that you have authority over my death and my life, is not true. You have authority to kill the body, but we, the servants of Christ and worshipers of the cross, do not count that as death; rather it is true life that does not die. Over my soul and my life, which is in Christ, you have no authority at all. Our Lord encouraged us and commanded us in his Gospel, saying: 'Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul; fear rather me, who am able to destroy both soul and body in Gehenna.' Still, if you wish me to speak with you, calm your anger, quiet your spirit, listen to me kindly, and order that I be struck no more." Then Qardagh swore to him, saying, "Say whatever you wish, and no one will strike you again." The holy Abdisho answered

and said to him, "Do you agree that whatever is self-existent and was not made is the true God?" The marzban said, "Yes, I agree." The blessed one said, "And do you acknowledge that whatever was made and was not self-existent is a creature?" The marzban said, "Yes, I acknowledge that." Again the blessed one said, "And do you know that creatures ought not to be worshiped, and that whoever worships created things angers God their Creator?" The marzban said, "Yes, my lord, you have spoken truly, and so it is. But show me: who worships creatures?" The blessed one said, "You and all your fellow pagans worship creatures." The marzban said, "If you show me that I worship creatures and anger God, I will gladly agree with you and follow your teaching, and I will count it as the greatest kindness on your part. But if you do not show me, know well that you are vexing me sorely." The blessed one said, "Do you not worship the sun and the moon, fire and water, air and earth, and call them gods and goddesses?" Qardagh said, "Yes, I worship them, because they are self-existent and not made." The blessed one said, "Where then did you find that the luminaries are self-existent and not made?" Qardagh said, "From their constant course, from the unchangeableness of their nature, and from the fact

that they remain in the strength of their nature and do not change as other things do, and that they are set on high." The blessed one said, "The things you have mentioned they received from their Creator when they were established; they are not their own achievement. That they are not self-existent is clear from the fact that they are not even alive. And if you say that they are alive, let me ask you, and you answer me: what kind of life do they have? That of animals, or that of rational beings? If they have the life of animals, why are they not fed like animals? Or are they perhaps rational and discerning? If you call them rational and discerning, how is it that they do not hold back their heat at the right time and rest from their course? For if the sun were rational, in winter it would break the force of the cold, and in summer it would not increase its heat; in a place colder than another it would give warmth, and where it is hot it would hold back its rays; and in its constant course it would grow weary and suffer. For whatever lives and is seen to move of itself also grows weary. And whatever does not live and does not tire is moved by something else. A stone, an arrow and a wheel are moved by others and do not tire, because they are not alive. But birds

and animals move of themselves and do tire, because they are alive. So if the luminaries and the elements moved of themselves, they would tire and suffer, since they are visible things. But because they do not move of themselves—as it is plain that they are mute and soulless—they do not tire, but are moved by the life of others, like a stone, an arrow and wheels. The one group is moved by God—that is, the luminaries and the elements; the other by us—that is, the stone, the arrow and the rest." The marzban said, "Then why do they possess, more than the things on earth, constant motion, and a light and a power that keep them from change, destruction and decay?" The blessed one said, "Because they hold the rank of the principal members in a body, such as the brain, the heart and the liver. If someone removes a nail, a hair or a tooth from the body, it is a partial loss; but if someone removes the brain, the heart or the liver, then together with these goes the destruction of the whole life. In the same way, if one of the lesser parts that sustain the world perishes, such as animals and seeds, it is a partial loss. But if the Creator allowed the luminaries to perish, the destruction of the whole world would follow.

For the luminaries are the strength of the whole body of creation; they are its principal members, the eyes and the brain of the world. From them comes all the warmth in bodies and in roots, the ordering of the seasons, and the reckoning of years, months, weeks and days. Yet they do not possess these things by their own authority; they received them from the power and wisdom of their Creator, and they are neither alive nor sentient. If ten people are in a single house and one of them suffers an injury to his eye, he alone is afflicted with darkness, while the others are free of pain. But if you put out the lamp in the house or shut the door, the experience of darkness reaches everyone in the house. Such is the loss of the other things compared with that of the luminaries. From this it is shown that the luminaries are not self-existent but made, and that they are neither alive nor sentient. Whoever worships them angers God their Creator. So too the elements—I mean earth, water, fire and air—are made, and are neither alive nor sentient. How can things be called self-existent that dissolve and destroy one another, so that the victory of each is the defeat of another? Earth is dissolved by water and even swept away by it. Water is swallowed up by

the earth and disappears, and it is also drawn up by the air. Fire is quenched by water and perishes. Air is shut up in a skin, is heated by the luminaries, and becomes mixed with foulness and damp. In short, each of them by its very nature destroys whatever belongs to another. They dissolve and change, and they need one another. Whatever is in need has come into being, and whatever has not come into being is not in need. For just as the uncreated is in no way in need, so everything that has come into being is in need. That the elements need one another, experience itself bears witness: none of them can sustain itself without another. Earth needs water to be fruitful; water needs air, which lifts it up and scatters it. And fire, without wood—which grows from earth, water and air—cannot show its power. So it is shown that they are in need. And if they need one another, they have also come into being. For the uncreated needs neither itself nor anything else. The uncreated is also living and rational, but the elements are neither living nor rational. For whatever lives

and is visible moves of itself and has feeling. The elements are not only without reason; they are also without life and without feeling. Plants and animals have life: plants grow and bear fruit, and animals have movement and change of place, along with the discernment of the senses. But the elements have none of these; they are as silent as stones. Whoever worships them and considers them self-existent angers God their Creator. So I was right to call you worshipers of creatures and strangers to God." When the marzban heard this, he grew very angry, for his error did not allow him to be persuaded by the blessed one's words. He ordered holy Abdisho to be bound in heavy fetters and shut up in a dark house, and to be given a little bread from one evening to the next, but no water. So the saint was bound and shut up, rejoicing and singing: "The Lord is my helper; I will not fear. What can man do to me?" The next day the marzban went out to hunt. He drew his bow to shoot an arrow, and it fell at his feet. The same thing happened to the servants who were with him. Though they tried many times, the air would not carry the arrows they were shooting.

When this happened to them, they were seized with great fear. The marzban spoke up and said to those who were with him, "I think that the old man we have bound is a man of God, and it is through his prayers that this wonder has happened and our weapons have been rendered useless, because we have caused him grief." At once he turned back and went into his house in great distress, and passed the night without eating or drinking. He resolved in his mind to release the blessed Abdisho at dawn. At midnight a great and glorious light filled the house where the blessed Abdisho was bound, and a great company of spiritual beings appeared to him, singing with loud voices: "The righteous cried out, and the Lord heard them and delivered them. The Lord is near to those who call on him in truth; he does the will of those who fear him, hears their prayer and saves them." The blessed Abdisho too sang with them, rejoicing. Great fear fell on all who were near the house where the blessed one was bound. At once all the doors opened, and an angel of the Lord came to the blessed one's fetters, and the fetters fell from his hands and feet. The angel took him by the hand, led him and brought him out of the prison. When he had brought him outside, he let go of his hand and said to him, "Come

after me." And he went ahead of him in shining garments until he had brought him into his cave; then he left him and departed. At dawn the marzban ordered that the saint be released and brought before him. When those who had been sent opened the doors and went in, they found the fetters lying there by themselves, and the fragrance of sweet spices filled the whole house. They searched for the blessed one, and when they could not find him they were astonished and filled with great fear. They ran quickly and told the marzban, "My lord, we went as you commanded and found the doors shut. We opened them and went in, and found these fetters lying there, and the house was full of the fragrance of perfumes, but we did not find the man." When the marzban heard this, he was overcome with great fear and distress. He struck his face and wept bitterly, saying, "Woe is me, woe is me, woe is me, for I have mistreated the man of God! Truly great is the God of the Christians! He is the true God, who made heaven and earth and all that is in them, and there is no other God besides him!" At once he rose and went into the summer house, drew the sign of the cross on its eastern wall, fell on his face to the ground, and prayed before it, saying, "Christ, God of

of the Christians, answer me, seek me out and do not reject me. Make me worthy to be numbered among your worshippers and to be signed with the holy seal. For I have believed and confessed, and I confess, that you are the true God, as your worshippers the Christians confess and teach. If, then, it was a human being who appeared to me in human form and spoke with me in your name, and I provoked him without knowing it, make me worthy, Lord, to see him again and ask his forgiveness for my folly, and through his hands to be brought near to knowledge of you and to your household. And if the one who appeared to me in human form was one of your holy angels, let him appear to me again and teach me what is right for me to do.” As soon as he had finished his prayer and sealed himself with the sign of the cross, a sweet and gentle voice was heard, saying to him: “For everyone who asks receives, whoever seeks finds, and to the one who knocks the door is opened.” When he heard that voice he was comforted and rejoiced greatly. His soul was glad, and he praised God. Then he went out and sat on his couch, took food and was strengthened. Now whenever he ate, the magus who used to recite the magian grace over him was amazed and wondered at him, along with his wife and all the members of his household, because he was eating bread without the magus reciting the grace for him.

But no one dared to question him, for he was very harsh and stern toward the members of his household. Three days later the holy Mar Abdisho appeared to him in a vision of the night, joyful and cheerful, and said to him: “My son Qardagh, if you wish to see me, come to such-and-such a cave, and there you will find me.” When he awoke from his sleep he rejoiced greatly and his soul was glad. At dawn he rose joyfully, changed his clothes and disguised himself. He took with him two faithful servants of his, men he trusted to keep his secrets, who were also made worthy of the gift of baptism along with him. He mounted and rode joyfully to the region of Beth Bgash, to the mountain where the holy Abdisho lived, the place he had appointed for him in the vision. When he had gone about five miles from his fortress, Satan met him in the form of an old man, angry and gloomy, chewing his beard with his teeth, and said to him: “Where are you going, you liar of wicked life? Why have you lied to me, abandoned me and gone after that accursed one in white garments, the disciple of Jesus, whom his fellow Jews crucified in Jerusalem, and he died? I swear, and I am not lying, that I will denounce you to the king

and to all the nobles of Persia, and I will have your blood shed like that of bandits and evildoers.” When one of his servants heard this, he said to his master: “Shall I draw my sword and plunge it into the head of this old dog who dares to vex our lord?” Then his master said to him: “Leave him alone, for he does not fall before the sword. Our Lord Jesus Christ, in whom I have believed, will destroy him with the breath of his mouth and bring him to nothing by the appearing of his coming. That is what I have heard the Christians say about him.” Now the holy Mar Qardagh had perceived that it was Satan who had appeared to him in human form. At once he spat at him and said: “May Christ my Lord rebuke you, he who in his goodness rescued me from the darkness of error, called me and brought me near to the great light of knowledge of him.” And he sealed himself with the sign of the cross. When Satan heard the name of Christ, he was immediately transformed and became like a black snake, and he fled and slipped into a cleft in the rock. The blessed Qardagh rode on his way, rejoicing and praising God. When he was at an inn on the road, the holy Mar Sergius the martyr appeared to him in a dream and said to him: “My brother Qardagh, you have begun well. Fight valiantly, so that you may be

my brother forever. Behold, I am with you to help you until you are made perfect and receive the crown of martyrdom.” The next day, toward evening, as he was beginning to reach the foot of the mountain where the holy Abdisho lived, the angel of the Lord appeared to the holy Abdisho and said to him: “Rise, go out to meet Qardagh the marzban, and receive him joyfully, for he is my chosen one, says the Lord, and he is mine, and he will suffer many things for my sake.” So the holy Abdisho rose joyfully, took his staff in his hand and the holy book of the Gospel on his left arm, and as he walked he sang: “They go out weeping, those who carry the seed; they come back with joy, those who carry the sheaves.” When he saw the blessed Qardagh from afar, he called out to him cheerfully: “How very weak your fetters are, my lord marzban! To us who are bound by the Holy Spirit and are traveling to heaven they count for nothing. Still, this is how the nobles and lords of the world receive the strangers who come to them.” The blessed Qardagh answered him with great joy: “Though we bound you while we were in error, you have released us from the fetters of paganism and drawn us

to come and ask your forgiveness. And you, like a merciful father, ask our Lord for pardon for the sins we have committed before him.” At once he got down from his horse and fell at the feet of the holy Abdisho, weeping and saying: “Forgive me, my lord, servant of God, and entreat Christ my Lord to make me worthy to be filled with his love.” The blessed man took him by the hand and said to him: “Get up.” He got up, and Abdisho kissed him and said: “Come in peace, my son, whom I begot in my bonds. Our Lord Jesus Christ is waiting for you, and his holy angels rejoice over you.” Then the young men took the horse to a monastery at the foot of the mountain, having been ordered not to say who the animal's owner was, while the two of them climbed up to the cave where the holy Abdisho lived. When the hour came, the blessed Abdisho rose to sing the evening office, and the blessed Qardagh stood beside him with awe and great joy. And behold, a band of bitter demons appeared on the cliff above them, dancing, clapping their hands and laughing, and saying: “Oh, how fine it is for the patakhsha and marzban to leave his house, his honor, his authority and his greatness, and spend the night hungry among the crags with deluded men

who live in caves!” The blessed Abdisho did not break off his office, but signaled to the holy Mar Qardagh to give them a fitting answer. So the blessed one answered them: “At all times you are liars and the fathers of lying. Yet this you have said truly: it truly is fine for the patakhsha and marzban to delight in the spiritual nourishment, full of true life, with holy men by whose words your cunning schemes have been defeated, who have left the earth and are running toward heaven. When I delighted in defiled tables and polluted wines, as your unclean will desired, I was stripped of the pure table of life that is in Christ and was far from God. And I had become a companion to you dark and rebellious [?] ones, who are reserved for that endless torment. But today, since Christ my Lord has made me worthy of the light of knowledge of him, behold, I delight in the spiritual table of his holy teaching. As for you unclean ones, go to the outer darkness!” At once they vanished, wailing and crying out and shaking the mountain. When the blessed men had finished their office and sat down, the holy Abdisho said to the blessed Qardagh: “See, my son, we have

a few soaked chickpeas here and a little vinegar in a gourd. Let us eat, my son, and drink water.” Qardagh answered him: “Whatever your will desires, father, I will gladly do.” When they had prayed and begun to eat, behold, the angel of the Lord appeared to them and said: “Peace be with you.” And as he spoke he held out his hand, carrying a loaf of baked bread, and said to the blessed Qardagh: “When we came to you, you bound us in iron and gave us bread without water, just enough to keep us alive. But today, now that you have come to us, see, we have lodged you on high and beautiful mountains, we have brought you baked bread, and here is cool water flowing on the mountaintop. But come in peace, for there is great joy among the angels and among men at your coming to us.” He placed the bread on the table and vanished. At once the blessed men rose, and both of them knelt for about three hours, praying, rejoicing and praising God. When they had finished their prayer, they ate what had been sent to them from heaven, and the whole night they were diligent in the service of God. Now there was an old man, advanced in days, whose name was

Beri. He lived in a cave about nine miles distant from the cave of the blessed Abdisho. He was a great and godly man, and he had lived on that mountain for sixty-eight years. The Lord said to him in a vision: “Rise, go to Abdisho's cave and see Qardagh the marzban there. Encourage him by your presence and strengthen him by your word.” The old man rose with great joy, and as dawn broke he reached Abdisho's cave. When Abdisho saw him he was astonished, for in sixty-eight years he had not come out of his cave. The old man said to Abdisho: “See, you have a great guest. Why did you not invite us to the feast along with him?” Abdisho said to him: “Forgive me, father. I said to myself that I would not trouble your old age, which could not even have made the journey.” The old man said to him: “Even though you did not invite me, the Lord sent me.” They prayed and gave each other the greeting of peace. Then the old man took hold of Qardagh, kissed him and said: “Come in peace, Esau the man of the field, who has been transformed and become Jacob the blameless, and dwells in the tent of the righteous.” He sat and spoke the word of God with him until the ninth hour; then he blessed him, kissed him, rose and returned to his cave.

When the blessed Qardagh had stayed five days with the holy Abdisho, he entreated him earnestly night and day to make him worthy of the seal of baptism. In the night before the sixth day dawned, the holy Mar Sergius the martyr appeared to Abdisho in a dream and said to him: “Why do you delay to open the gate of martyrdom before my brother Qardagh?” When Abdisho woke from his sleep he was struck with great fear. He called the blessed Qardagh and said to him: “Rise, my son. Let us go down to the monastery where the young men are and carry out what I was commanded this night.” As they were coming down from the mountain, the blessed Abdisho told Qardagh the vision he had seen in the night. When they reached the monastery, the brothers gathered and prepared the baptism, and, rejoicing and exulting, he and his two servants received the seal of Christ and partook of the holy mysteries. After receiving the seal of baptism he stayed seven days with the holy Abdisho. Then he set out and returned to his house, exulting in the faith of Christ. While he was at an inn on the road, Satan appeared to him in the form of a magus, with his clothes torn, wailing and weeping and saying: “Why, my son Qardagh, have you abandoned me and clung to my enemies?” The blessed one

answered him boldly: “I trust in the power of Christ my Lord that I will snatch many from your destroying jaws and bring them to the house of worship of Christ my Lord.” Satan answered him: “You have poor men living on cliffs, but I have the kings and nobles of all Persia. Since you have lied to me, I am going to inform the kings and rulers, and I will make you die a bitter death.” The blessed Qardagh sealed himself with the sign of the cross and said to him: “May Christ my Lord destroy you, he for whose love I am ready to suffer and to die gladly.” At once Satan was transformed and became like an old Ethiopian, with his hands on his head, wailing, weeping and fleeing. When the blessed one reached his house, he sent for a solitary brother worthy of good remembrance, named Isaac, and had him brought to him. Isaac taught him the psalms of the blessed David and read to him from the book of the holy Gospel. From then on the blessed one kept his mouth from eating meat, and he sustained himself from evening to evening with a sparing meal, stripped of the flavors of rich foods. He opened his treasuries and distributed great gifts and abundant alms to churches, monasteries and holy convents, to the poor and the needy, to orphans and widows; and crowds

of the sick constantly gathered before him and at his door. But his wife, his parents and all the people of his household were deeply distressed to see all the abundance he was giving away. The blessed one called them and said to them: “Why are you so sad, you foolish people, over earthly possessions that are being exchanged for those in heaven? Listen, if you are willing, to the life-giving gospel of our Savior, who cries out: ‘Do not lay up for yourselves treasures on earth, where moth and rust destroy and where thieves break in and steal. For where your treasure is, there your heart will be also.’ If, then, you love me and are mine, where I am you too will be. But if you are not with me, then you are against me. And do not grudge my possessions, for I am giving them to Christ my Lord, who is the true King.” The saint grew quiet and gentle toward the people of his household and toward everyone, and rested from the wars and battles he had been accustomed to wage. He gave up hunting and the chase, the entertainments of the stadium and all other such pursuits, and occupied himself with fasting, prayer and the reading of the Scriptures. He was also diligent in hearing lawsuits, freeing the oppressed from

their oppressors and rescuing the wronged from those who wronged them, in all the regions under his authority. Now his father and mother lived in a village called Bar Hewton, because they had large estates and herds of horses there, and a famous fire temple which they had built and in which they lived. Not long afterward the blessed Qardagh turned it into a great monastery, which stands to this day and is called by his name. When his parents heard that he had become a Christian and was distributing his possessions and scattering his wealth among churches, monasteries and the poor, they were greatly grieved. His father said to the blessed one's mother: “Great is the evil that has befallen us, and we have become a curse among our peers. While we thought we had a good heir, we have begotten and raised the one who will uproot our house.” But his mother said to her husband: “It seems to me that we should not hinder him, but leave him to his own will and let him do as he wishes. We are already old and must die. The horses and estates are his, and he has authority over what is his. And who knows, perhaps the religion he practices is a good one? And if

we try to put an end to it, we will be committing a sin.” But her husband rebuked her and said: “Be quiet, you foolish woman! I think you too are a Nazarene, and it is you who have already driven your son out of his mind.” At once his father wrote to him as follows: “Even if you have hated yourself and despised your life and become a Nazarene, and have insulted our family and made us a disgrace among our peers, you have no authority to distribute the estates and horses of the fire temple to the Nazarenes.” When the blessed one received his father's letter and read it, he laughed heartily and said: “Our old man is very foolish, and he is running toward Gehenna.” And he wrote him a reply as follows: “Old man, you worship fire, and in fire you are destined to be tormented. But I will give my possessions to Christ, for with him I am destined to delight, in him I hope and on him I rely. As for the fire temples you boast in, I will soon make them into temples of Christ and set up splendid altars in them. I have no portion or inheritance with you, for Christ has called me and brought me near to himself and made me a son of his hidden Father.” But the wife of the holy Qardagh could not bear it, seeing the scattering of possessions and the distribution of gifts.

So she decided to write and inform her father, who held the rank and office of shahrkwast, Shapur Nikorgan. When she had written the letter and was ready to send it at daybreak, that very night there appeared to her in a dream a young man of handsome appearance, dressed in white, sitting on a golden chair at the gate of the blessed one's fortress. He held a pen of fire and was writing letters on a broad white sheet [?], sealing them with his ring, and sending them up to heaven by the hands of handsome young men, dressed in white garments and flying on wings of fire. When she saw that fearful vision, and the young men going up to heaven and coming down to carry the letters, she approached him and asked him: “Who are you, my lord? What is your work? Why are you sitting here without the marzban noticing you? And what are you writing?” He answered her: “I am the chief of the hosts of the Lord God, who made heaven and earth. The great King of the ages has sent me to record the gifts and alms which

your husband gives, and to send their account up to heaven. As for what you said, that the marzban does not notice me, you are quite mistaken. The marzban knows me and is aware that I am here. It is you who do not know me, because your heart is on earth.” When she woke from her sleep she was in great fear, and she ran trembling to the blessed Qardagh and told him what she had seen. She also showed him the letter she had written in the evening to send to her father. He said to her: “Truly great, fearful and true is the vision you have seen; it is your own concerns that harden your heart. Our Lord said in his gospel: ‘I have come to set a man against his father, a daughter against her mother, and a daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law; and a man's enemies will be the members of his own household.’ All this, until even between a man and his wife, who are one flesh, there is to be a rift and division. This is what he said in another place: that on the day when he is revealed in glory and brings about the resurrection, justifies the righteous and condemns the wicked, two will be in one bed: one will be led up to heaven, to the kingdom and to delight, and the other will be left on earth, in Gehenna and in torment. But I trust in Christ my Lord that I too shall soon go to him, following my possessions.” From that day on

his wife no longer dared to say anything to him, nor did she again show a sullen face about the dispersal of possessions the blessed one was carrying out. When two years and three months had passed, while Qardagh was conducting himself in all the virtues befitting true Christians, the hostile peoples of the south and west heard of the change in the blessed one's way of life. They learned that he had withdrawn from wars, given up battles and come to love a life of quiet, and they all made ready together, Romans, Arabs and the other peoples around them, gathered like the sand on the seashore, and set out to invade the regions under the blessed one's authority. A few days earlier he had gone up the mountain to his master Mar Abdisho. When he had stayed with him for a month, while the two of them were keeping an intense fast with the holy old man Beri the mourner, great Roman and Arab troops took captives from and laid waste all the regions under the blessed one's authority, from the river Turmara as far as Nisibis, the frontier city. They also took captive his father and mother, his wife, his brother and sister, and all the people of his household.

But two hundred and thirty-five horsemen of his own retainers escaped and hurried to the mountain, looking for the blessed one. They went and found him in the cave of Beri the mourner, with his master Abdisho and a large gathering of priests assembled in his honor. When the blessed Qardagh saw them, he immediately spoke first and said to them: “You look to me like fugitives from the army.” One of them, a man coarse in his ways and wicked in his paganism, answered him: “When patakhshas and marzbans live in the caves of bandits and deceivers, this was bound to happen to us.” As he spoke, the angel of the Lord struck him, and he fell where he stood and died. When his companions saw what had happened, they were struck with great fear, and they all believed in our Lord Jesus Christ and received the seal of holy baptism that same day. Then the blessed Qardagh said to the holy and blessed Beri and Abdisho: “My fathers and lords, pray for me as I go, so that by the power of Christ our Lord and by your prayers I may bring back the great body of captives from the plunderers.” They sealed him with the sign of the cross, kissed him and sent him away in peace.

When he reached his fortress above Melqi and saw the ruins thrown down, and his house plundered with no one left in it, he was deeply grieved. At once he sent swift messengers after them, and wrote to them as follows: "You supposed that I, Qardagh, had stripped off my former strength in the might of war, and so you dared to enter and lay waste the regions under my authority. But know this: I have not stripped it off at all. Rather, I have put on a strength that cannot be overcome. Now send me all the souls you have taken captive; keep the property for yourselves, and go in peace. Do not stir up war with me; this is to your advantage." When they received the letters and read them, they wrote back to him insults, abuse and words of mockery. He wrote to them again, as follows: "Since I have put on Christ, the peace of the world, I do not wish of my own will to put on the wrath of wars. But send me my father and my mother, my wife, my brother and my sister, and all the people of my house, and all the captives you have led away from the regions under my authority. Keep the property for yourselves, and turn aside and depart from me. Do not make me pursue you." When they heard

these things, trusting in the fact that they had already come near the regions under their own authority, they cut off his brother's head and sent it to him. When the blessed one saw his brother's severed head, he was changed by grief and kindled with anger. At once he gave the order, the horn was sounded, and he went into the church of God with two hundred and thirty-four attendants and seven of his servants. He stretched out his hands and prayed, saying: "Judge my cause, O Lord, and fight against those who fight against me. Take hold of weapon and shield, and rise up to help me; draw the sword and flash it against my pursuers. Say to my soul, 'I am your savior.'" When he had finished his prayer, he took the blessed dust from before the sanctuary and scattered it over his weapons, his horse and his attendants. He hung on his neck the golden cross in which was set a holy piece of the wood of our Savior's cross. Then he lifted up his hands and raised his holy gaze on high, and made a vow to the Lord, saying: "Lord God, mighty one, hero of the ages: if you will be with me on this road on which I am going, and if by your power and your help I overtake my enemies and defeat them, and take back from them the captives they have seized, and return in peace from the battle

that is set before me, then I will uproot the fire-temples and build shrines of the martyrs. I will overthrow the fire-altars and set holy altars in their place. The young sons of the Magians, who have been set apart by their fathers as servants of Satan, I will give as servants to Christ and make them sons of the covenant. And the treasures and endowments that my fathers set apart and gave to the fire-temples I will distribute to the churches and monasteries." When he had finished the words of his vow and the terms of his promise, behold, a voice was heard from the sanctuary of the Lord, saying: "Take heart, take heart; be strong and of good courage, and do not fear, my servant Qardagh. For I am with you, and I will deliver your enemies into your hands." When that voice was heard, he and his attendants at once fell on their faces before the ark of the Lord, for about two hours. Then they rose with joy and praised God. The holy man gave the order, the horn was sounded three times, and they mounted. Then one of his armor-bearers said: "But, my lord, we do not know the road by which we should pursue our enemies." The blessed one laughed cheerfully and said to him: "He who let us hear the voice of victory will show us the straight road by which we shall go

and pursue and overtake our enemies." When they had ridden about two miles, behold, strips of silk from his wife's garments lay thrown on the road. She had acted with great wisdom: throughout the whole country through which the captors led them, at every parasang or every two parasangs, she would slip away secretly from the captors, tear strips from the silk of her clothing, and throw them on the road, so that they would be signs and tokens for her husband in his pursuit of them. For she trusted in the valor, strength and tender love of her husband, that he would not be slow to pursue the captors. When the blessed one saw this, he rejoiced greatly and praised God. Following those tokens they rode on until they drew near the regions of the Qardu. He lifted up his eyes and looked, and behold, great camps of the enemy were encamped on the river Khabur. They were encamped in confidence, eating and drinking and singing, rejoicing and making merry over the great captivity and the rich spoil that was in their hands. Then the blessed one dismounted from his horse, he and his attendants, and they fell on their faces on the ground. And he prayed, saying:

"Heavenly King of kings, to whom belong the unchanging kingdom, power, authority and might in heaven and on earth; by whose power Joshua son of Nun laid waste great and strong kings, and by whose uplifted arm blessed David conquered the nations all around him: help our weakness, so that your great name may be glorified in the victory of your worshipers for ever and ever. Amen." And all his attendants answered with one voice: "Amen." The blessed one gave the order, and they sounded three great and terrifying blasts on the horns. At that very moment the holy Mar Abdisho, his teacher, appeared to the blessed Qardagh, holding the glorious sign of the cross in his hand and running before him, and he said to him: "Behold, my son, the great sign of your victory. Only be strong and of good courage, for the Lord has delivered your enemies into your hands." Suddenly the victorious one rushed upon the enemy like terrible lightning, like the sun at its rising, and like a hero who rejoices to run his course. Three times he cried out with furious shouts and said to them: "This is the day of retribution for your insolence, you unclean dogs!" And at once he blazed into battle. All the captives ran to meet the blessed one and got behind him.

The camps were scattered before him, and he cut them down like ears of grain in a field. Their corpses fell into the river Khabur like worthless thorns, and a few of them escaped on foot to the mountain. He struck them and pursued them as far as the foot of the mountain on whose summit Noah's ark came to rest. Then the holy one returned with great victory and joy, singing and saying: "Some trust in chariots and some in horses, but we shall be strong in the name of the Lord our God. They have bowed down and fallen, but we have risen and stand firm, for the Lord our God has saved us." He turned back and plundered the camps, carried off the spoil, and brought back all the captives. When they came to their lodging place, he gave the order and the horn was sounded. All his attendants gathered, and he reviewed them and found that every one of them had been kept safe from harm. As soon as the blessed one reached his house, he gave orders, and the fire-temples that his fathers had built were uprooted, and he made them into holy temples to the Most High. He overthrew the fire-altars on which the erring Magians had kindled fire, and set up shining altars to Christ. Everything he had vowed to the Lord he accomplished and fulfilled with great

joy. When the Magians in the regions under his authority saw all these things, they wrote and secretly informed a certain Magian who was called the Mowbed of Mowbeds. He at once went in to King Shapur and said to him: "My lord king, live forever! Qardagh, who was so greatly honored by your majesty, and whom you made governor of Assyria and marzban in the western land, has gone over to the religion of the Christians. He has uprooted the fire-temples and built churches and monasteries. He flogs Magians and makes them Christians. He despises the worship of the gods, insults the great teaching of Magianism, and regards your kingdom as a widow who has no husband." When the king heard this, he said to him angrily: "How is it that you have heard these things, and have not heard of the great victory Qardagh won, how with two hundred and thirty-four men he destroyed thousands of Romans and tens of thousands of Arabs?" When the Magian heard these words from the king, he was shaken and became afraid; he fell silent and said nothing. Distressed and gloomy, he went out from the king's presence, and went and gathered all the nobles of the kingdom and stirred them up with his words, so that together they would accuse the blessed Qardagh before the king. Then they all gathered, and with one voice sent

to the king, saying: "Our lord king, if it pleases your gracious will that paganism be corrupted and abolished and that we all become Christians, command that your will be made known to your servants, so that we may know what we ought to do. But if this is not so, why have you been negligent about the insolent Qardagh, who, behold, despises the gods, uproots the fire-temples, and builds houses of worship for the evil religion of the Christians?" When the king heard these things, he was deeply grieved, for he loved the blessed Qardagh with all his soul. But because of the will of the nobles, he was compelled to summon the blessed Qardagh. He at once gave orders, and a letter was written to the holy Qardagh as follows: "We have heard of the victory and the mighty deeds you performed against the Romans, the Arabs and the rest of the peoples who dared to enter our territory, O our good servant. Therefore it has pleased us to delight in the sight of you and to reward you with honor in return for your great victory. As soon as you see this letter of ours, come with haste to our gate, and do not delay." For the king was afraid to tell him openly about the matter, lest he rebel, cause a disturbance and shake the kingdom. When the blessed one received the king's letter and read it, he smiled gently and said to the man who brought it: "What this letter says is not

what is in the king's heart. Yet in truth he has said that I am to receive great honors and precious gifts from his hands, and I am ready to go with great joy." At once he went into the church, spread out the letter before the Lord, and prayed, saying: "Christ, Son of God, who with your pure blood purchased your Church and freed it from sin, and made me, a sinner, worthy to belong to your household: strengthen my weakness to stand firm in this great contest set before me. Grant that I may come out of it victorious, and die for your name with my mouth full of thanksgiving to you and of praise for your holy name." Then he sealed himself with the sign of the cross and set out, praising God. When he drew near the king's gate, the king sent to him secretly and said: "Behold, the Magians and all the nobles of the kingdom are pressing hard against you and want to kill you, because they have heard that you have abandoned Magianism and the worship of the gods and become a Christian. But when you come in before me, do not say that you are a Christian, so that your accusers may be put to shame and we may honor you with great honors. And once you return to your land and your domain, be as you wish."

At daybreak the blessed one was ordered to come in before the king. As he was going in, all the Magians and the nobles of the kingdom gathered and stood there, threatening him and gnashing their teeth. But the blessed one looked at them modestly and sang gently, saying: "All the nations surrounded me, and in the name of the Lord I cut them off. They hemmed me in and surrounded me, and in the name of the Lord I cut them off. They surrounded me like bees and blazed like a fire of thorns, and in the name of the Lord I cut them off." When he came in before the king, the king called out in a loud voice and said to him: "Welcome in peace, pure servant, glory of our kingdom! We have heard of your victories and have highly praised your valor, and we are ready to reward you with honor. Yet we have heard something that troubles us greatly, and if—God forbid!—it is so, you deserve a bitter death. For they say that you have abandoned the great religion of Magianism, insulted the gods, joined the Christians and become a Christian." And while the king was saying these things to him, he was signaling to him with his eyes to deny it and say, "These things are not true, and I am not a Christian." But the blessed Qardagh secretly called on God to be his helper. And he recalled in his heart the saying

of blessed David: "I will speak of righteousness before kings and will not be ashamed." He opened his mouth boldly and said to the king: "In truth, my lord king, I am truly a Christian. I have confessed and I confess, in secret and in public, that I am a Christian. And by the power of Christ my Lord I defeated the enemies and destroyed the camps of the captors who dared to come against the regions of your territory, which you entrusted to me." When the king heard these things, he was deeply grieved. But because of the nobles of the kingdom, he changed his face to anger and wrath, and said to the holy man: "Since you have denied before us the gods who govern heaven and earth, and have confessed Jesus, whom the Jews crucified, we too will renounce our love for you, wipe out affection for you from our mind, and hand you over to death, and to bitter deaths." Then the nobles and all the Magians raised their voices and cried out, saying: "This man deserves ten thousand deaths!" But the king at once ordered that he be bound hand and foot and sent to his own land, and be judged there. He did this thinking that perhaps, after being held in bonds for a long time, he would repent, deny Christianity, and live. The chief Magian, however, kept urging that Qardagh be handed over to him, so that he might judge him as the greatness of his folly deserved. But the king did not

answer him, because he wanted to keep the holy man alive. The king gave orders and handed him over to a hundred horsemen, fifty foot soldiers and twenty nobles, to take him to the regions in which he had held authority, so that he might be judged there. And he wrote a letter to Gushnazdad and Dingushnasp, the mowbeds of those regions, as follows: "Qardagh, who hates his own life, who was greatly honored by us, as you know, whom we made governor and appointed marzban in those regions, has denied the gods, despised our kingdom, insulted our religion, confessed Jesus who was crucified, and become a Christian. Behold, we have sent him to you in harsh bonds and with trustworthy guards, ordering that he be given a period of seven months for reflection and repentance. If within the appointed time he does not distance himself from the evil religion of the Christians, and with his own hands and the hands of the people of his house uproot the churches and monasteries he built, and rebuild the fire-temples, and purify himself with the Magians, and hold the barsom, and perform the Magian rites for the gods, and worship the sun

and the moon and the fire, we order that he be stoned with stones at the door of his house. His blood be on his own head, and we are innocent of his blood." When the king's writings reached the mowbeds Gushnazdad and Dingushnasp, and they read the document written concerning the holy Mar Qardagh, they rose in haste and brought him to Burzmihr, who held authority from Nisibis westward; for he was a general and lived on the frontier. When they reached Nisibis, and this Burzmihr heard of it, he gathered all the Magians who were in the city, men of note, and they went out to meet him and brought him in. All of them kept urging him to return to paganism and to remain in his position of authority, in accordance with the king's command. But he said to them: "From now on I am a Christian, and I do not worship the sun and the moon as you do." When he would not be persuaded by them, they set out to take him to Shahrkhwast the judge, who had been appointed by the king over this matter, so that anyone who denied Magianism would be handed over to him. By the time they arrived opposite the monastery of the holy Mar Jacob, it was already evening. Many pagans

lived along that river near the monastery of the holy Mar Jacob and in the villages around it, and this Shahrkhwast lived there too. He was exceedingly wicked in his paganism, and had inflicted many tortures on Christians to turn them to paganism. He came out to meet the holy Mar Qardagh, and when he saw him he said to him: "I do not bow to you, because you have abandoned Magianism and become a Christian. Yet be persuaded by me: worship the sun and the moon, purify yourself with the Magians, and hold the barsom as was your custom. If not, you have much to suffer at my hands." The blessed one said to him: "May Christ, whom I confess, rebuke you, you wretched dog!" When he said this, the judge became furious. At once the judge gave orders, and they put chains and iron fetters on his forelimbs [?]. He ordered them to bring instruments of torture and set them before him: hooks, branding irons, an iron comb, and the rest of the other instruments of torture. They put an iron chain on his neck, and loaded him with many fetters and bonds. And that very night there appeared to him the holy Mar

Abdisho, his teacher, and Beri the mourner, and the blessed Mar Sergius the martyr, and they said to him: "Take courage and do not be afraid, Mar Qardagh." Then he was freed from those bonds, and he rose and prayed with the saints. They encouraged him, sealed him with the sign of the cross, and departed. Until morning came he did not cease from his prayer and supplication to God, and he was ready to receive the beautiful crown of martyrdom in that very place. He prayed before God thus: "Lord God almighty, King of kings and Lord of lords, make me worthy to be numbered among your worshipers and to be joined to the assemblies of those who praise you. And whoever comes and takes refuge in this place, asks for prayer and remembers my name here, may every request he makes be granted to him from the treasury of your mercy. Whether it concerns the sickness of people or of beasts, may he find health and healing from the abundant wealth of your goodness." When morning came, all the pagans gathered and threatened him, saying: "If he does not worship the sun, we will put him to a bitter death." But he said to them: "Get away from me, you sons of Gehenna! I worship Christ the King,

who is God of gods and Lord of lords." When the judge heard this, he wanted to have him killed there. But the king had commanded that if within seven months he did not repent and turn to Magianism, purify himself with the Magians, rebuild the fire-temples he had uprooted, and hold the barsom and perform the Magian rites, he should be stoned with stones in front of the door of his house; so they could not transgress the king's command and kill him there. Nor were the mowbeds willing to allow this. Instead, they brought him straight to his house, so that he might die there according to the king's command. When the blessed one came near his fortress beside the village of Melqi, he lifted up his eyes and saw his fortress and his house. He raised his gaze to heaven and stretched his sight on high toward God, and prayed, saying: "Christ my hope, who gave your body to the cross, and your hands and feet to the driving of nails for the redemption of our race, and who freed Adam and his children from the bonds of death: free me too from these bonds, and deliver me from the erring nations, so that those who hate me may see it and be put to shame, because you, Lord, have helped me and comforted me." At that very moment the bonds fell from his hands

and from his feet. He turned and worshiped toward the east, and stretched out his hands to heaven and gave thanks to God. When the nobles, the pagans and the foot soldiers saw what had happened, some of them fled in haste and scattered in every direction, while others ran and hid among the reeds and rushes of the lake beside the blessed one's fortress. But he went up to his fortress and entered his house, rejoicing and praising God. He encouraged his wife, his sister and all the people of his house, and gave orders for guards and posted watchmen on the wall of his fortress. When this became known to the king, he was greatly troubled; he gnashed his teeth in his anger and roared like a ravening lion. At once he wrote a letter to Burzmihr Shapur, general of the West, ordering him to send troops of horsemen to capture the blessed one's fortress and seize him, and to stone him in front of his fortress. And if the blessed one was not seized and his fortress taken by the horsemen he sent, the general himself was to come with his whole army, fight against the fortress and capture it. The general at once sent twenty troops of soldiers, and they besieged the blessed one's fortress for a whole month, but achieved nothing. Many of them died

in the fighting. For he flashed down on them like mighty lightning from the wall of his fortress, and with his sharp arrows he struck down many. Then the general himself came with his whole army, and achieved nothing. So they wrote and informed the king: "If he is not caught by stratagems, tricks and persuasion, he will not be taken by force and battle." The king gave orders and the armies withdrew; ten troops remained, stationed two and three miles away from the blessed one's fortress. Then, by the king's command, the nobles of his family gathered to persuade him to give himself up, so that his fathers and brothers would not perish on his account. When they had gathered and come, the blessed one went up onto the wall of his fortress and said to them: "Why are you troubled, men? And why have you gathered?" They bowed down to him from afar, and all wept with one voice and said to him: "Have pity, my lord, on yourself and on us too. Do not stand against the king, and do not bring an evil name upon our renowned family. Rather, order the gate of the fortress to be opened, and come out to us. Obey the king's command, and worship the fire just once

and the sun [?], and save our lives. Deliver us too, and afterwards be as you wish." But the blessed one opened his mouth and said to them, "If only you too were as concerned for yourselves as I am concerned for you! Because I truly care for my soul, I have taken it out of the snare of error in which you are held, and I have brought it near to Christ, the light of the world. And I am ready to endure many deaths for the sake of his holy name. If you are persuaded by me, you too will be made worthy along with me. As one band of martyrs we will offer ourselves to Christ God, we will be raised up to heaven, and we will delight with him in that life which has no end. As for your saying, 'Do not stand against the king,' you have spoken truly like old men. For which is harder: that I should stand against a wretched man who today blazes and swells with pride and tomorrow is no more, or that I should stand against the heavenly King of kings, whose kingdom does not pass away and whose divinity does not change? As long as I was held in error like you and did not know Christ my Lord, the true hope of my life, I was subject to the impious and wicked king, and I fought valiantly in his battles. But now

that I have come to know Christ, who is the heavenly King and the true hope, I will not submit to erring and mortal kings, and I do not fear their threats." When they heard him insult the king and call him wicked and erring, they all cried out, stopped their ears, and said to one another, "Let us get far away, far away, and not hear blasphemy against the King of kings who is worshipped." But the blessed one laughed and said to them, "Truly you are wretched! You blaspheme against God, the Creator and Sustainer of the worlds, and offer the worship that is due to him to his dumb creatures, and you fawn upon a mortal man who is far, far removed from God." While he was speaking with them, Gushnazdad and Dinggushnasp [?], the mobads, came along with other magi. They approached the blessed one's fortress and said to him, "We do not bow to you, because you have insulted the gods, stood against the King of kings, and become a Christian. Nevertheless, hear what we have been commanded in letters by the King of kings concerning you. The merciful King of kings has commanded: Worship fire, sun and moon. Rebuild at once the fire-temples you uprooted, and uproot the churches and monasteries you built. Cleanse your soul in the assembly of the magi,

delight your heart with pleasures [?], live and do not die, and stand firm in your authority." The blessed Qardagh was incensed and said to them, "Shut your mouths, you unclean and abominable ministers of Satan! Far be it from me to abandon the true God who made heaven and earth and worship dumb creatures. To me the unclean commands of your impious king are no better than the blasphemies that demons insolently utter against God." When the magi heard this, they backed away, wailing and crying out, "Who can bear to hear blasphemy against the King of kings?" One of them, named Siyarzad [?], bent down, picked up dust from the ground, and threw it toward the blessed one, saying, "This is for that mouth which blasphemed against the gods and against the King of kings!" The blessed one signaled to one of his servants to give him a bow and an arrow. He bent his bow out of sight in the shadow of one of the battlements of the wall and set the arrow to it. He drew and struck that magus in the mouth; the arrow came out through the back of his head, and he fell and died on the spot. The blessed one laughed and said to him, "Take the reward for your love of your gods and your king." Then all the magi fled

in haste, wailing, and the nobles of his kin went away downcast. Then the blessed Mar Qardagh called one of them, named Anosh, a man renowned for his learning and his good conduct, and said to him, "Why do you suppose, Anosh, that I am afraid of dying for Christ and that this is why I stay in the fortress? Not so! Far be it from me—not so! To me, death for Christ is sweeter than the life of this present time. But until Christ himself commands me, in a dream or in a vision of the night, that the time has come for me to die for his name, I will not hand myself over to men sunk in error. I trust in the power of Christ my Lord that there is no one able to harm me. But when it pleases Christ that I should die for him, I will go out gladly and surrender myself to be killed." When these things became known to the king, he sent orders by letter to Nikorgan, the blessed one's father-in-law, to go and persuade him to open the gate of his fortress and give himself up. If he did not manage this, Nikorgan himself would suffer the bitter sentence of death. So Nikorgan came and camped beyond

the blessed one's fortress, about two bowshots away, for he was afraid to come any nearer to the fortress. He sent word to the blessed one to come up on the wall and speak with him. The blessed one went up, sat down facing him, and said to him, "Come closer, old man, and do not be afraid." When he came closer, he said to him, "Why are you distressed, Nikorgan? And why have you come here?" He wept bitterly and said to him, "I am distressed at the misfortunes that have befallen me: I have lost a son-in-law who had no equal among men. And now death threatens me too, if you do not open the gate of the fortress and give yourself up to me." The blessed one said to him, "Because your mind is lost in the error of demons, you think that I am lost. If your mind were not lost, you would see that I am not lost at all; rather, I have been found by Christ, the finder of the lost. It is you who are truly lost, for you have abandoned God the Creator and worship dumb creatures that were made for your honor and your delight." Nikorgan said to him, "Think of me as you wish, and insult me as you please; only save me from death, for the King of kings is angrily at war with me because of you. Do one of two things: either obey the king, abandon Christianity and turn

to Magianism, worship fire, sun and moon, rebuild the fire-temples you uprooted, and live; or else come out and die, as the foolish Christians die, so that we do not die because of you." The blessed Qardagh answered him, "I will not obey the impious and wicked king. I will not abandon the God who created me, redeemed me, sustains me, and will delight me in his kingdom, and I will not worship creatures as you do. I do not shrink from death for Christ; I will die gladly, and none of you will die in my place. If only you had that consolation, and would die for the sake of your own life! As for calling the Christians who die for the name of their Lord foolish, you have spoken out of the depths of your own folly. But be at ease, and have no grief or distress. I am now beseeching Christ my Lord to show me whether the time has come for me to die for his name. If it pleases the will of his divinity, and the time has come to receive the crown of martyrdom at the completion of this contest for his sake, I will gladly go out and give myself up to the executioners." Then the news spread through all the regions of the blessed one's dominion that Qardagh was ready to die for the name of Christ. Many crowds gathered and came from every region,

Christians, Jews and pagans, and camped in great encampments around the blessed one's fortress, waiting to see the day when the athlete of righteousness would be crowned. His parents and brothers came as well. The encampments grew great, numbering thousands and tens of thousands, and they stayed there, camped, for twenty-one days. The blessed one persevered in prayer and supplication, entreating Christ to strengthen and encourage him to be perfected with the crown of martyrdom. His father begged him many times with tears to come up on the wall so that he might see him and speak with him, and hear from him what he wished to say. He refused, but sent word to him through one of his servants: "Christ our Lord calls us in his gospel: 'Whoever does not leave father and mother, brothers and sisters, wife and children, and come after me, is not worthy of me.' For this reason I do not wish to see your face, because your thoughts and your words are opposed to the path on which I am ready to set out." After this Nikorgan sent to him: "Send me my daughter Shushan, for I long to see her." The blessed one said to his wife, "Go out to your father and see what he wants from you. But know this:

in his words a bargain is being struck for the ruin of your life." When she went out to her father, he said to her, "My daughter, my beloved, have pity on my old age. Do not exchange your father's love for your husband's affection, and do not sell the life of my old age for a man who has rebelled against the gods and against the King of kings. There is no way you can get another father; but if your husband dies today, by morning you can find a better one than he. So persuade him to open the gate and come out, so that we may be saved from danger." At once she turned to the blessed one and said to him, "If you are a Christian, come out boldly and die bravely, as Christians die. Why are you shut up in the fortress like a coward afraid of death, while many are dying because of you?" The blessed one answered her, "Truly the lips speak out of the treasures of the heart, as the life-giving word of our Savior says. These things you are saying are the evil devices of impiety, the fruits of wickedness, and the words of the deceiver. But do not mock, daughter of perdition, for I am ready to die, even in the face of your crafty enticements."

After all these things a fearful vision appeared to the blessed one. On the night before the dawn of Friday, the blessed one rose and performed the office as was his custom. When he had finished his office toward daybreak, he turned and saw himself standing on a small hill in front of the gate of his fortress, surrounded by great crowds of people who were scattering pearls over him. As the pearls fell on his body, drops of blood shone out from the places where they struck, and these turned into torches of fire and rose up to heaven. A man clothed in shining garments and crowned with a crown of light stood above him in the air and said to him, "My brother Qardagh." He said, "Here I am." He said to him, "These pearls were scattered over me too in Jerusalem, by the sons of my people and the sons of my tribe. Now your father will come and cast one pearl at you as well, and at once you will ascend to me in joy." The blessed Qardagh asked him, "Who are you, my lord?" He said to him, "I am Stephen the deacon, who was stoned in Jerusalem for preaching life." At once the blessed one awoke from his sleep, filled with great fear. He called Isaac his teacher, who used to teach him the psalms and read the holy scriptures before him, and he recounted

to him the vision he had seen. Astonished, they pondered the vision and understood that the time had now come for the blessed one to die beneath a heap of stones for the name of Christ. The blessed Qardagh said to Isaac, "Where is the story of this valiant martyr Stephen written?" Isaac said to him, "It is written in the Acts of the holy Apostles." The blessed one said to him, "Bring it and read it to me." When he heard the account of the martyrdom of holy Stephen, he rejoiced greatly and his soul was glad. He was encouraged and filled with great courage, and he longed for death for Christ as a thirsty man coming in from the road in the hot season of summer longs for cold water. Then the blessed one rose, knelt and prayed. He kissed the book of the holy Gospel and sealed himself with the sign of the cross. He opened the gate of his fortress and went out like a bridegroom coming out of the bridal chamber. When this became known to the crowds, a great commotion broke out in the encampments, and everyone ran in haste—Christians, Jews and pagans, great and small, men and women—running to see the blessed one receive the crown of martyrdom. Horsemen, mounted and armed, rode about, urging the crowds on

and telling everyone to take a stone and stone the blessed one. The magi gathered with all the nobles and sat reading out the written sentence against the blessed one which had been sent by the king—what the Church is accustomed to call a katarasis [?], and the Persians call a nibishtag. When the blessed one saw the crowds of pagans and Jews carrying stones and running to stone him, he looked up to heaven and sealed himself with the sign of the cross. He prayed in a loud voice and said, "Our Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, help me in this hour, and make me worthy to contend openly among the assemblies of your saints." Then he knelt. When a heap of stones had risen over him, he shook them off and stood up bravely. And he did the same a second time. As the horsemen and magi were urging the crowds to throw stones with force, the blessed one answered them, "I will not die unless my father throws a stone at me." His father, drunk with the errors of Magianism, afraid of death, and fawning on the king and the nobles, took

his veil, wrapped it over his face, and threw a stone in the stoning of his son. At once the soul of the athlete of righteousness departed to eternal life. In that very hour a fragrance of spices spread through the whole place where the blessed one had been stoned, and a voice was heard saying, "You have fought well, and valiantly have you won the victory, victorious Qardagh. Come in joy and receive the crown of your victory." The holy Mar Qardagh was crowned in the forty-ninth year of King Shapur, on a Friday. On the night before the dawn of Saturday, compassionate men gathered, snatched the holy one's body from its guards, and buried it with great honor. Every year, on the day on which the blessed one was crowned, the people would gather at the place where he was crowned and hold a feast and commemoration for him for three days. And because of the size of the crowds, they even began to buy and sell on the days

of the saint's commemoration. As time went on, a great festival came to be held at the place where the blessed one was stoned, and so it is to this day: the commemoration of the saint lasts three days, and the fair six days. It is called the Market of Malqi, after the name of the village of the blessed one's fortress. Afterwards a great and beautiful church was also built, at great expense, in the name of the blessed one, by faithful people worthy of good remembrance, together with that hill on which the holy Mar Qardagh was stoned. May we be made worthy by his prayers to be helped in this world full of sorrows, and in the new world that does not pass away to find mercy through his prayers and delight with him, by the grace and mercy of our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom, with his Father and the Holy Spirit, be praise, honor and exaltation for ever and ever. Amen. Here ends the martyrdom of the holy Mar Qardagh, the victorious martyr. (4) Afterwards the faithful brought gold and silver and built four churches for him, and another church, a martyrs' shrine, with an altar, a chancel and a baptistery. It was consecrated in the eastern quarter. Great sums were spent on it in the name of the blessed one by faithful people worthy of good remembrance. Whoever keeps his commemoration on the day on which he was stoned, may he be made worthy to have a portion and a good end with that blessed one, to be helped in this world, and in the new world that does not end to find mercy through his prayers.
